channel.title: Daily Recap — 📟Tech News
channel.description: What happened in 📟Tech News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: One of Google's Android partners secretly turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
item.description:
Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor into 1.3 million set-top boxes and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and cut ties with the manufacturer, Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices.

It's a striking supply-chain story: the compromised boxes were certified Android TV devices, sold through normal channels, with the backdoor baked in at the factory. For Google, the episode is a black eye for its certification program; for owners, a reminder that cheap streaming hardware can carry hidden costs.

Sources

  • The Verge: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet

item.title: Meta will end Quest 2 and Quest Pro OS updates in 2027
item.description:
Meta will release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, with version 213 as the final major release. After that, the company will continue shipping security patches and critical bug fixes through the end of 2027.

The Quest 2 was the headset that brought VR mainstream, selling tens of millions of units, so the end of feature updates marks the close of an era — even if the headsets themselves will keep working. Owners who want new features will need to move to Quest 3 or later hardware.

Sources

  • The Verge: Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027

item.title: BMW takes on Tesla's FSD with urban driver assist coming in 2027
item.description:
BMW says it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow. The system can help steer, accelerate, and slow the vehicle on highways and city streets using built-in GPS navigation.

It's a Level 2 system — the driver stays responsible — but city driving is a much harder problem than highway cruising, with intersections, pedestrians, and unpredictable traffic. BMW's move puts it in direct competition with Tesla's Full Self-Driving in the market where automated driving is hardest to get right.

Sources

  • The Verge: BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027

item.title: Ford promises never to sell your driving data to data brokers
item.description:
Ford has vowed never to sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers, part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics data without authorization.

The promise is as much a competitive jab as a policy: several automakers have been caught or sued over quietly passing driving behavior — braking, speeding, late-night trips — to insurers and brokers. Ford is betting that an explicit, public 'never' is worth more than the data revenue it's forgoing.

Sources

  • The Verge: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers

item.title: OpenAI pitches data-center power plants as grid protection
item.description:
OpenAI announced its Grid Protectors Program, piloting at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies — enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.

The announcement lands as opposition to data centers grows in communities worried about grid strain and electricity costs. OpenAI's pitch reframes its massive power appetite as a civic asset: a data center that can shed load on demand, acting as a shock absorber for the local grid rather than just another drain on it.

Sources

  • The Verge: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas

item.title: Anthropic clamps down on Claude's AI video game clones
item.description:
Anthropic has updated Claude Code's system prompt to prevent the tool from being used to re-create existing video games. Retro gaming is currently awash in AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, and while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make original games, it doesn't want its tool used to clone existing ones.

It's a notable line-drawing exercise in AI copyright: the same capability that lets someone build a new game lets them reproduce an old one, and Anthropic is choosing to police the distinction at the system-prompt level rather than wait for lawsuits to do it.

Sources

  • The Verge: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones

item.title: Who's falling in line for Trump's 'Super Intelligence' loyalty test
item.description:
At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with a single directive: government agencies must rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as 'Super Intelligence.' MIT Technology Review now tracks who is falling in line — and the compliance map is revealing.

The rebrand is more than semantics. The order effectively turns a piece of administration vocabulary into a loyalty test, and the outlets, agencies, and companies that adopt the term — versus those that quietly don't — are signaling where they stand with the White House. In an industry that lives on government contracts and regulatory goodwill, the choice of one word has become a political act.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test

item.title: Xbox's former COO breaks silence on her abrupt departure
item.description:
Helen Chiang, Xbox's former chief operating officer, has said she has 'serious concerns' about her abrupt departure from Microsoft less than two weeks ago. Chiang left after 21 years at the company, having been promoted into the COO role only in July, with a surprisingly short farewell memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma.

The brevity of that memo — and the speed of the exit — has fueled speculation about what happened inside Xbox's leadership. Chiang's public comment doesn't explain the departure, but it confirms that whatever happened, she doesn't consider it a clean break.

Sources

  • The Verge: Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure

item.title: NASA asks commercial space to help save Hubble
item.description:
Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without an orbit boost it will burn up in the early to mid 2030s. NASA is now taking proposals from the commercial space industry to help save the famed telescope — a shift from the government-only rescue thinking of the past.

The stakes are high: Hubble remains scientifically productive decades after launch, and a commercial reboost could buy years of additional science for far less than a replacement observatory. It's also a test case for whether private spaceflight can take on heritage-mission stewardship, not just launches and cargo.

Sources

  • The Verge: NASA hopes the commercial space industry can help save Hubble

item.title: Flock keeps ignoring cities' requests to cancel its contracts
item.description:
More cities are voting to cancel contracts with Flock Safety, the license-plate-camera company — but canceling turns out to be hard. Plymouth, Minnesota voted to terminate in September, yet Flock failed to respond to the city's request, and the cameras stayed up for over a month.

The pattern matters beyond one city: surveillance infrastructure is easy to install and hard to remove, and vendors that drag their feet on cancellation effectively extend surveillance past the democratic decision to end it. Expect this to become a template dispute as more councils reconsider their Flock deals.

Sources

  • The Verge: Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contracts

item.title: North Korea linked to the massive Binance crypto heist
item.description:
North Korea has been linked to the massive Binance crypto heist — the breach behind the $6.3 billion theft that Binance spent the weekend recovering from. Attribution to North Korean actors fits a long pattern of state-linked crypto theft funding the regime.

The scale is what stands out: multi-billion-dollar exchange breaches are no longer outliers, and the laundering and recovery fight now plays out in public, in real time. For crypto users, the incident is another argument for self-custody and for treating even the largest exchanges as points of risk.

Sources

  • The Verge: North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist

item.title: A fully playable Portal prequel, F-Stop, has leaked
item.description:
A fully playable version of F-Stop, Valve's unreleased Portal prequel, has leaked — giving players a chance to experience a piece of Valve history that never shipped. F-Stop was an earlier prototype whose mechanics evolved into Portal 2's gel system and other ideas.

Leaks like this are catnip for game historians: playable prototypes reveal how a classic was built, which ideas survived, and which were cut. Valve has historically tolerated this kind of archaeology more than most studios, and the community response will likely be preservation and analysis rather than piracy panic.

Sources

  • The Verge: A fully playable version of Portal prequel F-Stop leaked

item.title: HomePod Mini 2 first look: three things to love, one disappointment
item.description:
A first look at the HomePod Mini 2 finds three things to love and one disappointment — with Siri, smart-home chops, and its role as a Mac speaker in the spotlight. The mini remains Apple's most approachable smart speaker, and the update refines rather than reinvents it.

For anyone deep in the Apple ecosystem, the Mini 2's appeal is the same as ever: cheap enough to scatter around the house, good enough to actually use. The single disappointment is worth checking before you buy — it may be the difference between an upgrade and a pass.

Sources

  • The Verge: HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment

item.title: New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
item.description:
A new column argues that the latest Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists — blockbusters built on timelines, budgets, and creative conditions the current industry can't reproduce. The piece reads the two giants as artifacts of an era when studios could spend years and fortunes on a single title without the live-service pressures that dominate today.

It's a bittersweet frame: these games may be the last of their kind, not the start of a new wave. For players, the takeaway is to appreciate them on their own terms — and to expect the next decade's biggest games to look structurally different.

Sources

  • The Verge: New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists

item.title: California's Prop 45 could hide a loophole for data centers
item.description:
California's Proposition 45 could contain a loophole for data centers, according to a new analysis — potentially letting energy-hungry facilities sidestep rules voters thought they were tightening. Data centers' power demands have become a flashpoint in state energy politics, and the fine print matters enormously.

If the loophole is real, it would let some of the state's biggest new electricity consumers operate under lighter scrutiny just as California strains to decarbonize its grid. Expect the measure's supporters and opponents to litigate the interpretation hard before ballots are counted.

Sources

  • The Verge: Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers

item.title: Apple's HomeView could add security camera features
item.description:
Apple's HomeView could gain security camera features, The Verge reports — echoing separate reports that the device can already behave like a HomeKit camera. Turning a home hub into a security camera would give HomeView a clearer job in the home and a sharper edge against rival displays.

The question is privacy positioning: Apple has built its brand on on-device processing and user control, and a camera in the living room tests that promise in a very literal way. How Apple frames the feature — and what stays on-device — will matter as much as the feature itself.

Sources

  • The Verge: Apple's HomeView could add security camera features

item.title: Binance CEO: 90% of stolen crypto has been replenished
item.description:
After hackers stole a record $6.3 billion from Binance customers, the company's CEO says 90% of the funds have been replaced, with the remaining 10% — in less liquid tokens — also planned to be covered. Binance is covering the losses directly from company funds.

The scale of the heist made it one of the biggest in crypto history. That Binance can absorb it says something about the exchange's balance sheet — and about how much risk still concentrates in centralized exchanges.

Sources

  • The Verge: Binance CEO says 90 percent of stolen assets have been ‘replenished’

item.title: Nintendo declares November 1 Pikmin Day, with Pikmin 4 news for Switch 2
item.description:
Nintendo announced that November 1 will be the first annual Pikmin Day, revealed in a short Pikmin Day Direct. Shigeru Miyamoto shared new information about Pikmin 4 for the Switch 2, an update for the mobile app Pikmin Bloom, and a new series of Hello! Pikmin shorts.

It's a small celebration for a beloved, offbeat franchise — and a sign Nintendo is keeping Pikmin in the spotlight as the Switch 2 builds its library.

Sources

  • The Verge: Happy Pikmin Day Eve

item.title: Windows 11 tests new Xbox-mode shortcuts and smarter search
item.description:
The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode — controlling Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and power settings without leaving the game — plus comprehensive search improvements, including filters for files, actions, and web results.

For handheld gaming PCs and living-room setups, the Xbox-mode shortcuts are the more meaningful change: fewer trips out of the game just to toggle a setting.

Sources

  • The Verge: Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search

item.title: Why you can't escape unhinged political texts
item.description:
With the midterms days away, political texts have reached peak intensity — breathless fundraising pleas, attack ads, and even celebrity-recorded appeals landing on voters' phones. The Verge digs into why these messages are so relentless and so hard to stop.

The mechanics are the story: campaigns exploit loopholes in spam rules, peer-to-peer texting platforms, and the fact that blocking one number just means the next one arrives. If your phone feels like a campaign rally, that's by design.

Sources

  • The Verge: Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts

item.title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
item.description:
Meta wants to sell you a Muse Charm this holiday season — a squishy AI companion you carry like a Tamagotchi. One Verge writer wasn't buying one, because they already built their own: a Waveshare ESP32 gadget running Claude, vibe-coded into existence.

The DIY version captures the same idea — a small, cute, always-there AI helper — without the $100-plus price tag or the ecosystem lock-in. It's also a neat illustration of how accessible this kind of hardware project has become.

Sources

  • The Verge: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could

item.title: Best Buy bundles a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
item.description:
The new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is up for preorder at several retailers, but Best Buy is sweetening the deal with a $100 gift card automatically added to your cart on 14- or 16-inch models.

It's the best preorder sweetener spotted so far for Apple's highest-end laptop, and a useful offset if you were already planning to buy.

Sources

  • The Verge: Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders

item.title: Apple Intelligence finally comes to China with iOS 27.3
item.description:
Apple will launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3, the company announced on its Chinese newsroom website, as reported by MacRumors. The features arrive first in an iOS 27.3 beta set to launch November 4, with the full release scheduled for December.

China has been the conspicuous gap in Apple's AI rollout, held up by regulatory requirements around AI services. Closing it matters commercially — China is one of Apple's largest markets — and it sets a precedent for how US tech companies navigate Beijing's AI rules.

Sources

  • The Verge: Apple Intelligence is finally coming to China with iOS 27.3

item.title: AI giants back a shared opt-out standard for web scraping
item.description:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard letting publishers opt out of AI scraping across multiple companies at once, rather than setting preferences individually. The shared "policy token" signal, reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable, applies a publisher's AI training preferences broadly.

The agreement is notable for its breadth: the four biggest AI labs aligning on one mechanism gives publishers a single lever instead of a patchwork. It doesn't settle copyright disputes, but it could defuse one of the web's longest-running tensions — sites feeling scraped without consent — if the standard is honored in practice.

Sources

  • The Verge: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping

item.title: Google's satellite AI server sends its first response back to Earth
item.description:
Google's AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post, Google said it successfully booted the satellite's Tensor Processing Units, letting the on-board Gemma 4 model answer a prompt with a haiku about being in space, looking down at the blue marble below.

The test is an early step in Project Suncatcher, Google's bid to run AI inference in orbit rather than beaming raw data to Earth. If it scales, satellites could process imagery and sensor data on board, sending back answers instead of terabytes — a potentially transformative shift for Earth observation and space-based computing.

Sources

  • The Verge: Google's satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth

item.title: Starbucks explores AI-personalized menus at the drive-thru
item.description:
Starbucks is exploring drive-thru experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless, CEO Brian Niccol said during an earnings call. The idea is to tailor what you see on the menu board to your tastes and history.

It's the latest sign of AI moving from back-office efficiency into the customer-facing moment of ordering. The pitch is convenience — your usual, surfaced faster — but it also raises the usual personalization trade-offs: the more the menu knows about you, the more it shapes what you choose.

Sources

  • The Verge: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru

item.title: Rivian's autonomy gamble faces its first real test
item.description:
On an hourlong earnings call, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time on the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than on hyping the company's still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions. The crucial test comes later this year, when Rivian rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature.

The emphasis is a gamble: Rivian's near-term fortunes ride on shipping the R2 at volume, but Scaringe is betting investors' attention on autonomy instead. Whether the hands-free rollout lands cleanly will say a lot about whether Rivian can credibly play in the same league as the established self-driving players.

Sources

  • The Verge: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test

item.title: Altman: RAM belongs in data centers, not on your desk
item.description:
Asked about supply chain shortages, including the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on the Cheeky Pint podcast that it is "terrible" to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. His argument: scarce memory should go where it does the most AI work.

The comment lands as memory prices squeeze PC buyers and builders, with AI data center demand soaking up supply. Altman framing consumer RAM as a misallocation is blunt — and self-interested, given OpenAI's own appetite for data center hardware — but it captures the core tension in today's chip market: AI infrastructure and personal computing are now competing for the same silicon.

Sources

  • The Verge: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk

item.title: Eating disorders are rising — and GLP-1s could make things worse
item.description:
GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade — but to some clinical psychologists, they can also be a potential trigger for eating disorders. A new report suggests the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up by 71% between 1990 and 2023, and clinicians worry that drugs that suppress appetite could compound the risk for vulnerable people.

The concern isn't that GLP-1s are inherently harmful — they help millions — but that their normalizing of appetite suppression can mask or accelerate disordered eating. As prescriptions surge, the report argues, screening and support for eating disorders need to keep pace with the drugs' adoption.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
  • MIT Technology Review: The Download: GLP-1s and eating disorders, self-aware cities, and forever chemicals

item.title: Patrick Stewart dies at 86
item.description:
Patrick Stewart, best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men, has died at age 86. A message posted to his Instagram account said he died at his Los Angeles home on Wednesday following what it called a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.

Born in 1940 in Mirfield, Yorkshire, England, Stewart built a career that spanned Shakespearean theatre and blockbuster franchises, becoming one of the most recognizable screen presences of his generation. Picard alone carried him through The Next Generation, four films, and a later streaming revival, while his Xavier anchored two decades of X-Men films. His death closes a chapter on an era of genre storytelling he helped define.

Sources

  • The Verge: Patrick Stewart has died at age 86

item.title: Reddit will require logins — and says Google's AI search isn't sending traffic
item.description:
Reddit announced a major shift alongside its third-quarter earnings: it will soon require everyone to log in, ending the era of anonymous browsing on a site long used as a crowdsourced answer engine. The move gives Reddit tighter control over who reads its content and, crucially, over how AI companies scrape it.

CEO Steve Huffman also said Google's AI-powered search modes aren't helping: search referrals in October dropped by more than 1 million per day on average, echoing complaints from publishers across the web that AI answers are siphoning clicks. Taken together, the two announcements sketch Reddit's strategy for the AI era — lock down access, and push back on platforms that summarize its content without sending visitors.

Sources

  • The Verge: Reddit will force everyone to log in
  • The Verge: Reddit’s CEO says Google’s AI Mode ‘does not drive traffic’

item.title: Intel sells out of its affordable laptop chips
item.description:
Intel says demand for its budget-focused Wildcat Lake laptop chips is outstripping supply. CEO Lip-Bu Tan told investors the chips are effectively sold out, and CFO David Zinsner said the company has seen significant growth in the line, which arrives at what he called exactly the right time because it is cost-optimized.

The shortage matters because Wildcat Lake targets the affordable end of the laptop market — the machines most people actually buy. Strong demand there is a bright spot for Intel, but sold-out status also means laptop makers may struggle to keep budget models in stock, and buyers hunting for a cheap new machine could face delays or price pressure heading into the holiday season.

Sources

  • The Verge: Intel says it’s selling every affordable laptop chip it can make

item.title: Rivian's R2 is now its best-selling vehicle
item.description:
Rivian's third-quarter earnings brought a milestone: the smaller, cheaper R2 is now outselling all of the company's other vehicles for the first time. The company reported $2.155 billion in quarterly revenue, up 38 percent, as R2 production ramps.

The R2 has always been Rivian's most important bet — its ticket from a niche premium EV maker to a mass-market brand, and a key part of its software partnership with Volkswagen. Becoming the company's best-seller is the first real evidence that the bet is working. The open question now is whether Rivian can scale production and hold margins as the R2 carries more of the company's weight.

Sources

  • The Verge: Rivian’s R2 is officially its best-selling vehicle

item.title: GM to pay $220 million over selling drivers' data
item.description:
General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The deal resolves a complaint from a coalition of 36 state attorneys general and requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain drivers' express consent before sharing it.

The settlement is one of the largest of its kind for connected-car privacy, and it lands as cars collect ever more granular data about where we go and how we drive. For GM, the payout and the new consent requirements set a template other automakers are likely to face: regulators are treating driving behavior as sensitive personal data, not a free byproduct of owning a connected car.

Sources

  • The Verge: GM to pay $220 million to resolve claims it sold driving habits data

item.title: Gemini can now generate and edit files directly in chat
item.description:
Google's Gemini can now generate, preview, and edit files directly inside a chat — PDFs, Google Docs, Sheets, slide decks, Markdown, plain text, and code — without jumping to another app. The feature is rolling out to all Gemini users, with PDF preview and editing on web and mobile, while other formats are web-only for now.

The move turns Gemini from a chatbot that produces text into a workspace where documents are actually built and revised in conversation. That's a direct challenge to the way people use Docs and Office today: instead of asking an AI for a draft and pasting it elsewhere, you can iterate on the real file in place. For Google, it also deepens the tie between Gemini and its productivity suite — a combination rivals can't easily match.

Sources

  • The Verge: You can generate and edit Google Docs files directly in Gemini chats now

item.title: Climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
item.description:
Climate change is increasingly fueling more climate change — and our models may not fully account for it. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up temperatures, which in turn set off feedback loops that amplify warming further. Scientists have long warned about such loops, but a growing body of research suggests they are not fully captured in current climate models or in the emissions-reduction goals built on them.

The stakes are high: if feedback loops are stronger than modeled, the world could warm faster than projected, and the carbon budgets meant to keep warming in check could be too generous. The finding doesn't change the core prescription — cut emissions fast — but it suggests the margin for error is thinner than policymakers have assumed, and that some climate targets may already be out of reach.

Sources

  • MIT Technology Review: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot

item.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon, touting big gains in coding and cybersecurity
item.description:
Google has released Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model, with what it calls "significant gains" in coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity. Google says Carbon tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v5.0) benchmark, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra.

The launch matters because frontier-model leadership keeps rotating, and Google is explicitly pitching Carbon as a security-first model — a bet that enterprises will pay for AI that can both write code and defend systems. Expect rivals to answer with their own benchmark claims within weeks.

Sources

  • The Verge: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with a ‘significant leap’ in cybersecurity

item.title: Alphabet says AI is driving its fastest search growth yet
item.description:
Google parent Alphabet reported third-quarter earnings showing that its AI investments are translating into more searches, not fewer. CEO Sundar Pichai said AI is driving overall search query growth, including commercial queries, and that the year-over-year query growth rate is the highest the company has seen.

That cuts against the long-running fear that AI chatbots would hollow out Google's core business. Instead, AI features appear to be pulling more queries into Google — and more commercial intent with them, which is what advertisers pay for.

Sources

  • The Verge: Google says its investments in AI are driving more searches

item.title: Microsoft posts $92.3B quarter as cloud keeps climbing
item.description:
Microsoft opened its 2027 fiscal year with $92.3 billion in revenue and $33.6 billion in net income, up 19 percent and 32 percent respectively. The quarter also marks a change in how Microsoft reports its finances, with a new reporting structure alongside the strong cloud-driven results.

The numbers underline how durable Microsoft's cloud and AI bets remain: even as the company reshuffles its reporting segments, the underlying growth story is unchanged, and it sets a high bar for the rest of big tech's earnings season.

Sources

  • The Verge: Microsoft reveals strong cloud growth amid financial reporting overhaul

item.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro can cost $14,549 fully loaded
item.description:
Apple's newly announced touchscreen MacBook Pro — its first with an OLED display and touch — starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. Tick every premium hardware option Apple offers and the price climbs to $14,549.

The eye-watering ceiling is less about what most buyers will pay and more about how far Apple is willing to push pro pricing now that touch and OLED have arrived on the Mac. The base models are already a step up from the MacBook Pros announced earlier this year.

Sources

  • The Verge: Apple charges $14,549 for a fully specced touchscreen MacBook Pro

item.title: Hacker steals personal data of more than 41,000 DHS employees
item.description:
A hacker stole personal information on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees, including staff at Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection. The exposed data includes names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses, and office locations.

The breach is especially sensitive because it touches frontline immigration and border enforcement personnel, whose personal details are now circulating. It also raises fresh questions about the security of the systems holding federal workforce data.

Sources

  • The Verge: A hacker stole more than 40,000 DHS employee records

item.title: Anduril and Qualcomm promise a fully US-built laptop in 2027
item.description:
Defense contractor Anduril and chipmaker Qualcomm have partnered to build laptops entirely in the United States, starting with a single model in 2027 — and Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch. The companies also set a long-term goal of pushing the computer industry toward a fully domestic supply chain.

Even one made-in-America laptop would be a surprise given how thoroughly laptop manufacturing is concentrated overseas. Whether the effort scales beyond a niche defense-adjacent product is the real question.

Sources

  • The Verge: Anduril now says its BlueChip laptop will meet Buy American standards at launch

item.title: Instagram chief says public negativity toward AI is 'going to get worse'
item.description:
Instagram head Adam Mosseri acknowledged in an interview that a lot of people really don't like AI — and it's not just young people and creatives. Asked about the trend of college students booing tech CEOs at graduation ceremonies, he said the negativity around AI is "going to get worse."

The candor is notable coming from a senior Meta executive: it suggests the industry's biggest companies now expect public skepticism of AI to deepen rather than fade, even as they keep shipping AI features into every product.

Sources

  • The Verge: Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’

item.title: FCC's crackdown on Chinese gadgets widens beyond drones
item.description:
The US government's clampdown on Chinese-made tech is expanding from its original security worries into a de facto import ban covering consumer gadgets: drones, routers, and Roombas are among the first products facing restrictions, and they may not be the last.

For consumers, the practical effect is a shrinking set of choices in categories where Chinese brands have been dominant on price. For the industry, it signals that the trade and security fight is now reaching everyday devices, not just telecom infrastructure.

Sources

  • The Verge: Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech

item.title: Anthropic's IPO plan: take Wall Street's money, keep Wall Street at bay
item.description:
With its IPO prospectus now filed, Anthropic is trying to pull off a tricky balancing act: raise vast sums from public markets while insulating its safety-first mission from shareholder pressure. The company's elaborate governance structure is designed to keep investors from forcing it to cut corners as its models grow more capable — and more risky.

The 335-page filing devotes roughly 100 pages to risks alone, a sign of how seriously Anthropic takes the tension between growth and safety. Whether the structure actually holds once quarterly earnings pressure sets in will be one of the most-watched experiments in AI governance.

Sources

  • The Verge: Anthropic's elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
  • MIT Technology Review: The Download: Anthropic's IPO, smarter power grids, and exercise pills

item.title: iPhone Duo's foldable screen is already cracking at the hinge
item.description:
Within hours of the iPhone Duo's launch last Friday, buyers began reporting broken inner screens on brand-new foldables. Photos shared on social media show a consistent pattern: a crack or line appearing in the middle of the display, right above the hinge.

It's an unwelcome echo of early foldable teething problems, and the timing — day-one failures on a flagship device — puts immediate pressure on Apple to explain whether this is a manufacturing defect, a design flaw, or a limited batch issue. Expect a statement, and possibly a repair program, soon.

Sources

  • The Verge: Here's why the iPhone Duo's hinge could be cracking the screen

item.title: Meta hit with a $25 billion ruling in New Mexico kids-safety case
item.description:
A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to resolve claims that the company misled users around the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and failed to protect children — blowing past the $17 billion multi-state settlement attorneys general announced this summer, itself already unprecedented.

The ruling puts fresh blood in the water for Meta's legal exposure: if one state's claims can produce a figure this large, other pending cases could follow suit. It also sharpens the political case for stronger kids-safety regulation, with Meta now facing both courtroom and legislative pressure at once.

Sources

  • The Verge: Meta's $25 billion legal loss just put blood in the water

item.title: OpenAI touts science breakthroughs; researchers tire of the gatekeeping
item.description:
OpenAI announced impressive new results in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what it calls an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But researchers who spoke to The Verge say they're growing tired of the company's pattern: headline-grabbing claims with limited detail for independent verification.

The frustration follows a turbulent few months in OpenAI's relationship with the research community. The stakes go beyond academic etiquette — if frontier labs won't share enough for others to check their work, the field can't tell genuine breakthroughs from marketing, and public trust in AI science erodes.

Sources

  • The Verge: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs

item.title: Musk says Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms, after service slowdown
item.description:
Elon Musk claims Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using it for offensive drone strikes, saying the "loophole was closed last week" — his explanation for a recent slowdown in service reported earlier by Ars Technica. Ukrainian officials have denied that the alleged violation happened or that it caused the slowdown.

The dispute matters because Starlink remains critical infrastructure for Ukraine's military communications. A public fight over terms of service raises fresh questions about how much control a single private company — and its CEO — should hold over a wartime communications lifeline.

Sources

  • The Verge: Elon Musk says Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service

item.title: Firefox's Smart Window will now fill out forms for you
item.description:
Mozilla is adding AI form-filling and webpage monitoring to Smart Window, Firefox's AI-powered browsing experience. The new feature can pull information from your open tabs — say, your online portfolio or LinkedIn page — and paste your work history into a job application.

It's a practical, privacy-sensitive take on the agentic browser trend: useful automation without handing your data to a third-party agent. The question is whether users trust a browser with that much personal context, and whether Mozilla can keep the feature's data handling as private as its pitch promises.

Sources

  • The Verge: Firefox's Smart Window adds AI form filling and webpage monitoring

item.title: Solid-state transformers could help the grid survive the AI boom
item.description:
Transformers — the devices that move power efficiently across long distances — are in short supply, and their basic design hasn't changed much in a century. Solid-state transformers, which swap century-old copper-and-iron engineering for power electronics, could be the upgrade the grid needs as electricity demand from AI data centers surges.

The technology promises faster, more flexible power routing, but it's still early. Whether solid-state transformers scale in time to matter for the AI buildout depends on manufacturing, cost, and utilities' famously cautious adoption timelines.
